outputs.L1: They thought the field was going to waste, so they gathered the marker rocks and stones and piled them into a barn. They say the rocks were shaped, some etched with triangles and other forms, as though someone had been striving to invent a new language. They say those rocks went to build the wall that stands guard over the manor now, and a few were carried off for the state house. Still, the crops refused to grow. I say the stones marked an ancient tongue—one called eternity—and that it pointed toward the river. I say that after that collection was taken, no pillow in the big house dreamed again. I say that somewhere beneath this ground moulders one called Alice, whose great-grandson, himself old now, refuses to speak of slavery. I say that at the master's table, only a single plate is set for supper. I say no seed can flourish on ground once planted and then forsaken—yet wild berries warm a field of bones. Bloom how you must, I say.
outputs.L2:
They believed the land had gone unused, so they collected the boundary stones and rocks, stacking them inside a barn. Word has it these stones bore distinct shapes—carved with triangular marks and other symbols—as if someone had attempted to craft an unknown script. The stones, they claim, were later repurposed to construct the wall protecting the manor house, while others found their way into the state building's foundation. Nothing would grow in those crops afterward.

I believe those markings represented a forgotten language—one called eternity—oriented toward the water. I believe that once those stones were gathered up, sleep in the great house turned dreamless. I believe a woman named Alice lies decaying somewhere beneath this ground, and her great-grandson, now elderly himself, still won't speak of the days of bondage. I believe the master's dining table now holds just a single setting.

Nothing can take root in soil that's been cultivated and then deserted. Yet wild berries still give warmth across this bone-filled field—blossoming exactly as they're meant to, I believe.

# The Field of Stones

The field was considered wasted ground, unfit for planting, unworthy of the plow's attention. So when the decision came to clear it, no one questioned the logic: the marker rocks and stones that had rested there for generations—some for longer than any living memory could account—were gathered up like refuse. Rough hands pulled them from the earth where they had sat, undisturbed, and hauled them away to be piled into a barn, stacked without ceremony, without reverence, as though they were nothing more than debris cleared from a field before spring planting.

But these were not ordinary stones. Some had been shaped by patient, deliberate hands—worked and worn until they bore triangles, spirals, and symbols unlike any script found in ledgers or Bibles. They seemed to reach for something beyond simple markings, as if their makers had been trying to invent a language from nothing, or perhaps to preserve one that was already slipping away, syllable by syllable, from the mouths of those who once spoke it. Scratched into stone, the symbols endured longer than breath, longer than memory, waiting for someone who might one day understand.

Those who remembered the old stories—the ones passed down in whispers, in songs sung low over washbasins and cookfires—said the stones carried an old tongue. They called it eternity. It was said that this language, once spoken freely, had pointed toward the river, toward a way through or a way back, toward something the living needed to find. But over the years, the stones had been scattered—broken apart to shore up walls, hauled off to pave paths, even carried away to become part of the state house itself, unknowing monuments built from unmarked graves.

When the stones were finally uprooted from the field entirely, something in the land itself seemed to falter. The crops that were meant to flourish in that freshly cleared soil refused to grow, as though the ground remembered what had been taken and would not forgive the theft. And in the big house nearby, something else was lost as well: no one could dream any longer. Sleep came, but it came empty, without vision, without the strange comfort of encountering the dead or the future in the quiet hours of night. It was as if the stones had been holding open a door between the living and whatever lay beyond, and now that door was shut.

Beneath that same ground, still and silent, moulders a woman named Alice. She has been there long enough that her name survives only in fragments, spoken rarely, and always with a kind of careful hesitation. Her descendants remain in the area still—among them a great grandson, now bent and grey with age, who carries her blood but not her stories. He will not speak of slavery, not to strangers, not even to kin who ask. Whatever memories were passed down to him, he holds them close, sealed behind decades of silence, and it seems likely he will carry them, unspoken, to his own grave.

And so the field remains, its history buried twice over—once in the stones that were taken, and once in the silence that followed. Nothing marks the graves anymore, nothing but the wild berries that come up untended each summer, blooming bright and unbothered over a field that is, in truth, nothing more and nothing less than a field of bones.
outputs.L4:
# The Stones That Remembered

The field had lain fallow for three seasons before anyone spoke openly of why. It sat at the edge of town, bordered by the slow bend of the river, and for generations it had been known simply as "the old ground"—a place children were warned away from, though few could say precisely why anymore. The warnings had softened into superstition, superstition into inconvenience, and inconvenience, eventually, into opportunity.

It was old Henley who first suggested clearing the markers. He was a practical man, the kind who measured worth in bushels and board-feet, and he had grown tired of watching good land sit idle because of stones nobody could read anymore. The markers were rough-hewn things, some no taller than a man's knee, others rising to his shoulder, each etched with symbols that had long since passed out of memory. Spirals. Long unbroken lines that seemed to gesture toward the river's curve, or perhaps toward something further—the horizon, the sky, some idea of forever that the original carvers had tried to fix in stone because words alone could not hold it.

Nobody in the town could read the language anymore. That was the trouble. The markers had been standing so long, weathered by a hundred winters, that whatever meaning they once carried had eroded along with the sharp edges of their carving. They were just stones now—old, inconvenient stones sitting on land that could otherwise feed the town's growing hunger for grain, for pasture, for progress.

So the townsfolk came with wagons and crowbars. They worked through a long autumn, prying the markers from ground that seemed, some would later claim, reluctant to give them up. The earth around each stone was strangely compacted, threaded with roots that had grown around the bases as if embracing them, as if the land itself had accepted these stones as something that belonged to it rather than something placed upon it.

They didn't know—or didn't ask, or asked and didn't want the answer—that beneath that field lay the bones of people who had been brought to this land in chains. Generations of the enslaved had been buried there, in a plot set apart from the town's proper cemetery, marked not with names carved in the town's language but in a script brought from another place entirely, another world, transplanted here and passed down in secret even as the people themselves were stripped of nearly everything else. The markers had been raised by descendants who still remembered, who still carried fragments of the old tongue, who had carved into stone what could not be spoken aloud in the town proper: *this ground is sacred. These bones belong to the river and to forever. Do not forget us.*

But forgetting is easier than remembering, especially when remembering is inconvenient, especially when the ones who might insist on memory have no voice left in the town's affairs. The markers came down. Some were broken up for foundation stones. Others found their way into garden walls, into the base of the new grain silo, into the front steps of the schoolhouse—their spirals and lines now facing outward, upside down, sideways, meaningless ornamentation to eyes that no longer knew what they were looking at. The town congratulated itself on reclaiming useful land from superstition.

The field was plowed that spring with great optimism.

Nothing grew.

They tried again the following year, turning the soil deeper, bringing in richer seed, consulting the almanac for better timing. Still nothing—not even the stubborn weeds that colonized every other neglected corner of the county. The ground seemed to reject everything planted in it, as though something beneath had turned its face away. Cattle would not graze there. Even birds, townsfolk began to notice, flew wide of that particular stretch of sky.

They called it bad luck at first. Then, in whispers, they called it cursed.

The wild things did not share the town's forgetting. Blackberry brambles grew up thick and impenetrable around the field's borders, as though standing sentry. River birch seeded themselves in a loose ring that some claimed traced the exact boundary of the old burial ground, though no living person could have known where that boundary lay. At night, some swore they heard the river itself speaking differently as it passed that bend—not the ordinary rush of water over stone, but something almost like a language, patient and unbroken, still saying what the markers had once said in silence.

Mosses crept over the garden walls where the broken stones had been mortared in, softening their stolen edges. Ivy found the schoolhouse steps and would not be cleared away no matter how many times it was cut back, always returning, always tracing the same spiraling patterns that had once been carved by hands now generations gone. It was as if the land, stripped of its markers, had decided to become the marker itself—refusing to let the memory settle into the comfortable dust of forgetting, insisting instead on its own persistent, wordless testimony.

The town eventually stopped trying to farm that field. It stands empty even now, ringed by its brambles, watched by its birches, humming faintly with whatever the river still remembers. The stones that were taken remain scattered through the town's foundations and walls, holding up walls and steps for people who walk over them daily without a glance, without a thought for what they once meant, what they were meant to protect.

But the ground remembers, even when the people do not. And what is buried in erasure has a way of pushing back up through the soil, season after empty season—not as crops, not as anything useful in the town's old reckoning, but as a kind of testimony that refuses, stubbornly, to be plowed under.
outputs.L5:
# What They Thought The Future Would Hold

They thought the future would arrive with fanfare—flying cars slicing through silver skies, robots serving breakfast, cities gleaming with glass and light. This was the future imagined in old magazines and black-and-white films, a tomorrow built entirely from optimism and chrome.

They thought the changes would be obvious, dramatic, impossible to miss. Instead, the future crept in quietly, disguised as ordinary Tuesdays. It arrived in the glow of phone screens at 2 AM, in algorithms nobody fully understood, in conversations happening across oceans as if distance had simply given up.

They thought the problems of their time would be solved by now—hunger, war, loneliness—swept away by progress like dust before a broom. But problems, it turned out, were shape-shifters. They didn't disappear; they evolved, wearing new masks suited to new eras.

They thought the older generation just didn't understand, back when they were young and certain. Now, standing in similar shoes, they understood something else entirely: understanding was never really about knowledge. It was about distance—the particular vantage point that only time could provide.

They thought the answers would come easier with age, that certainty was a reward for living long enough. Instead, the questions multiplied, more nuanced, more tangled, until wisdom looked less like answers and more like comfort with not knowing.

Perhaps this is the quiet joke of existence: we spend our lives thinking the future is a destination, when really it's just an accumulation of present moments, each one surprising us in its own small, unremarkable way. The world rarely becomes what we imagined—it becomes what we didn't expect, which is often stranger, sometimes sadder, but occasionally more beautiful than anything we thought the future might hold.

down by the creek where the kudzu climbs

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical piece about a plantation's "wasted" field, where townsfolk explain away strange marked rocks, but the speaker insists the stones hold a language of grief and eternity connected to enslaved ancestors.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Field They Call Wasted

They say the field went fallow because the soil turned sour,
that nothing but Johnson grass could love that stubborn acre,
so they let it rest, let it run wild with chicory and thistle,
called it wasted, called it useless, called it empty.

They do not call it what it is.

The stones sit where the plow would not go,
low gray backs breaking the earth like something surfacing
for air after three hundred years underwater.
The county man says glacial till. Says erratic.
Says nature has her patterns, her leavings, her debris.

He is not wrong about the ice.
He is wrong about everything else.

I have run my palm along those markings—
not scratches, not the accidents of frost and thaw,
but lines that curve with intention, with the deliberate hand
of someone who had no paper, no ink, no permission
to write anything the world would keep.

So they wrote in stone.
So they wrote in the only ledger that would outlast
the men who owned their names, their children, their Sundays.

The historians want dates. Want documentation.
Want a signature they can trace to a parish record.
But grief does not sign its name—
grief makes a mark and moves to the next stone,
carries the weight of it to the next generation
who will stand here in October light
not knowing why their chest goes tight,
why their feet stop walking of their own accord.

This is not erratic.
This is architecture.

Somewhere under the thistle is a woman
who buried her third child before the frost,
who could not mark the grave with wood
because wood rots and this—this had to last
longer than mourning, longer than her own body
bent double in a field that was never wasted,
was never fallow, was never empty—

it was full.
It has always been so full.

The county says: let the deer graze there.
Let the milkweed have its way.

I say: listen.
The stones are still talking.
Some things refuse to be erosion.
Some things insist, in their granite silence,
on being remembered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem in fragmented, oral storytelling style—like folklore passed down—about markers stolen from a burial ground for building projects, ending with an image of wild berries growing over a field of bones.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Old Ones Say**

Listen—
they took the stones. Yes.
Took them for the schoolhouse steps,
for the mill's foundation, for
the rich man's garden wall—

*Grandmother's grandmother told it this way:*

The markers were gray as winter breath,
some carved, some plain,
some just river rock set upright
by hands that loved the dead.

Men came with wagons.
Didn't ask. Didn't need to—
the dead don't hold deeds,
the dead don't file complaint
in the county office.

*This is the part where the voice drops low:*

They said the ground was empty.
Said it was only field.
Said—and this is the lie passed down like a coin worn smooth—
said no one would miss what wasn't marked no more.

But the corn wouldn't grow right that year.
The well went bitter.
A child born blue and silent.
*You know how these things go in the telling.*

Some stones ended up in chimneys.
Warmed strangers' feet all winter
while below the frost line
old bones turned over, slow,
looking for what covered them.

*Skip ahead now—*

Skip the lawsuit that went nowhere.
Skip the marker put up after, cheap,
that said *Site of Former Burial Ground*
like the dead were a business
that closed.

Skip to now.

The field's gone wild.
No one plants it. No one builds.
Even the surveyors get lost
walking that particular fence line,
compass spinning like it forgot north.

But go there in July—

Go there when the sun's low gold
and the air smells like green things breaking open—

Brambles thick as a fist,
canes arched over like old women bowing,
and berries—

dark, dark berries,
so full they split their skins,
so sweet the birds get drunk on them,
so many that children fill their pails
and don't know why their grandmothers
won't eat what grows there,

why the old ones just stand at the fence
and watch the fruit ripen
over ground that kept its dead
the only way it had left—

by feeding something back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
